Issued at 313 PM CDT Tue Oct 20 2026

Breezy southerly winds will gradually decrease this afternoon and 
evening with mostly clear skies. Lows will fall to the mid to upper 
40s. For reference average lows this time of year are in the mid 
30s. Early Wednesday morning winds will become light, which may 
allow for patchy fog development along river valleys and low areas. 
Especially along the northern James River Valley where probability 
of visibility falling to 2 miles or less is around 50%. Any fog 
development will burn off by mid-Wednesday morning.

As for the rest of Wednesday an upper trough and surface low located 
over eastern Nunavut and Manitoba will drag a cold front into the 
region early Wednesday morning, connected to a secondary weak mid-
level shortwave and surface low over western South Dakota. At the 
same time moderate WAA on southerly winds will begin to amplify a 
shallow upper ridge located over the south central US. As this ridge 
continues to amplify through the day it will push back against the 
cold front causing it to stall out, eventually washing out the front 
and secondary low pressure. This will result in a diffuse weak 
surface boundary. Winds may vary along this boundary for a short 
time before becoming southerly once again as a surface high pressure 
strengthens over the central Midwestern states. By Friday 200 mb 
heights will be near to or at maximum for climatology, as will 700-
500 mb temperatures. What this means is at the surface we will be 
experiencing abnormally warm October days. The NBM continued showing 
a cold bias this run and so coordinated with neighbors to boost 
highs using a blend of NBM/NBM90th. Highs will rise into the low to 
mid 70s Wednesday, and the mid to upper 70s Thursday. There may even 
be a few 80s! While this is 10 to 20 degrees F warmer than average, 
we are still more than 5 degrees away from tying or breaking 
any record highs. 

Looking now to the west we see a deep upper trough moving on shore 
stretching from British Columbia down to southern California. As 
this and a series of embedded shortwaves on the west side of the 
ridge move east the SPG will begin to tighten. Southerly winds will 
increase, gusting 15-25 mph by Thursday afternoon for areas along 
and west of I-29. East of I-29 gusts will 15 mph or less. As this 
entire pattern shifts east overnight gusty winds will spread east. 
Friday winds will continue to increase, with widespread gusts of 30 
to 40 mph. Higher gusts are expected as you move west toward central 
South Dakota. Gusts west of the James River could reach 45+ mph.
While minimum relative humidity values will remain above 40%,
strong winds and drying grasses will lead to locally elevated
fire risk at times through the remainder of the week.  

In addition, early Friday morning WAA along the nose of the LLJ may 
result in light, scattered showers over south central South Dakota 
early Friday morning moving northeast into southwest Minnesota 
around noon. These showers are likely to be hit and miss, meaning 
not everyone will get rain, and those that do will probably only see 
a trace to a hundredth or two. Friday night into Saturday as the 
previously mentioned upper trough moves into the central plains of 
Canada and the US, draping a cold front down into eastern Colorado. 
Showers will form along the front and move southeast from early 
Saturday morning through Saturday evening. Once again showers are 
expected to be light, and could be spotty at times. A brief break 
overnight before a southern stream upper trough moves northeast into 
the region bringing more chances for rain Sunday afternoon into 
Monday morning. Overall totals are expected to be light, with areas 
of southeast South Dakota, northeast Nebraska, and northwest Iowa 
seeing around a 60% probability of 0.25 inches. Probabilities fall 
off quickly from there, and most will only see a few hundredths to a 
tenth or so.
